name: Catapult
description: A procedural siege catapult that teaches force and velocity vectors as a projectile launch. Two levers compose the throw — a LAUNCH ANGLE slider tilts the throwing arm and a FORCE slider sets the release speed — and a live dotted parabola previews where the stone will land before you fire. The launch velocity vector (green, from the basket) and the constant gravity vector (red, downward) stay visible: the arc is literally their sum. Press FIRE and the arm swings, hurling a RigidBody3D ball along the predicted path under gravity.
theoreticalGrounding: Projectile motion p(t) = p0 + v0*t + 0.5*g*t^2. The release velocity v0 = launch_direction(angle) * force is the entire initial condition; gravity is constant. Horizontal motion is constant velocity, vertical motion is constant acceleration, and together they trace the parabola. A throw is an initial condition — after release, physics decides the rest.

catapult.name: Catapult
catapult.description: Procedural wooden catapult: A-frame base, torsion pivot, a long throwing arm with a basket at the tip and a counterweight at the short end. A console with ANGLE + FORCE sliders and a FIRE push-button sits in front. Changing a control retilts the arm and redraws a live predicted-trajectory parabola; FIRE swings the arm and launches a ball that follows the arc. Always-on velocity (green) and gravity (red) vector arrows with labels make the parabola = initial velocity + constant gravity legible. DNA: throw sets the initial condition the machine is built for - mortar and flat turn the aim at unchanged force, heavy and weak turn the force at unchanged aim; foresight sets how much of the arc is previewed and vectors how the release is annotated. Use #throw:, #foresight:, #vectors:.
catapult.qfep_connection: F_force: a throw is an initial condition. You write direction and magnitude at release; gravity, constant and given, bends the rest. The parabola is the sum of what you give and what is given.

dna.default: foresight=parabola, vectors=sum, throw=balanced - the full dotted arc plus one velocity arrow and the gravity arrow is exactly what the 4 existing placements draw today; the component arrows are not even instantiated at that value, and throw=balanced is the else-branch of _apply_throw, which is character for character the two clamps _ready always ran (default_angle_deg 50, default_force 9.0) and never touches the counterweight. Scene tree and capture AABB unchanged
dna.was: the predicted parabola was always the whole flight path, and the throw was always drawn as a single arrow beside a single gravity arrow - both hard-coded in _update_trajectory and _update_vector_arrows with no way to say otherwise
dna.deepened: 2026-08-03 - added `throw`. foresight and vectors both draw the arc; nothing turned the arc itself. default_angle_deg = 50.0 and default_force = 9.0 were plain vars with no export, so although apply_grid_config would have accepted an #angle:/#force: token, no map has ever sent one: all 4 placements (ForcesArena, VFM_05_Launch, Zone_WarehouseLab, Zone_WarehouseLab_Packed) stand at 50 deg / 9.0 m/s and draw the identical parabola. A foresight axis over one arc is a preview of a foregone conclusion. The four values are a 2x2 around the shipped throw: mortar (75 deg) and flat (20 deg) turn the DIRECTION at unchanged force and bracket the 45 deg optimum from both sides - flat lands shorter than balanced, which is the half of that lesson a single arc can never tell; heavy (13 m/s) and weak (5 m/s) turn the MAGNITUDE at the unchanged 50 deg aim, where range goes as v^2. Direction and magnitude, one pair each, which is the artifact's own truth line.
dna.counterweight: the counterweight block was a fixed 0.26 m cube for every throw. It now scales with the cube root of force / 9.0 (mass goes as volume), so it is exactly 1.0 at the shipped force and moves only for heavy (1.13) and weak (0.82) - mortar and flat keep the shipped block, since they change the aim and not the force. The scaling is guarded on THROWS, so `balanced` never touches the geometry even if a map overrides the force through config. It deliberately does NOT track the FORCE slider: the counterweight is what the machine was built to deliver, the sliders are the aim taken with it.
dna.independence: throw is orthogonal to both older axes. foresight decides how much of the arc is drawn, vectors decides how the release is annotated, throw decides which arc exists at all. The arm tilt alone separates mortar/flat/balanced whether or not any preview is drawn, so throw still bites at foresight=none.
dna.harness_note: read the next bite report with this in hand. The sweep frames each variant from its own subtree AABB, and the trajectory ImmediateMesh is a MeshInstance3D whose vertices ARE the predicted arc - roughly 8 m against a 1.5 m machine at the default. That is why the wave-1 report shows subject_pct 3.41 (the machine is small because its own preview inflates the box) and why foresight=parabola vs none scored 3.48% while parabola vs apex scored 0.93%: turning the preview off collapses the AABB and re-zooms the whole tile. The same applies to throw - flat/mortar shorten the arc, heavy roughly doubles it - so part of any measured change is the camera moving, not the picture. It was kept anyway: a stronger throw honestly IS a bigger object, and the values were chosen to keep the range inside about 2.5 to 17 m rather than the 26 m a 45-degree full-force throw would have needed. A layers=0 framing anchor would pin the camera, but it would also inflate the measured footprint that sync_footprints.py writes, so it is left undone deliberately rather than by omission.
dna.framing_why: SOLVED, NOT GUESSED, by tools/solve_framing.py. At framing 1.0 this artifact's subject bounding box filled 30.0% of frame width and 25.1% of its height, with a subject share of 0.30%. The visible frame is 2 * PAD * radius * framing metres wide, so the box grows as 1/framing; solving for a target of 78% of the smaller-headroom dimension gives 0.32. THE ARTIFACT WAS NEVER DARK, EMPTY OR MISSING A FIXTURE - the camera was between three and eight times too far away, and the near-zero subject share this token had on record was a fact about the standpoint rather than about the axis.
